title: Do you need vinegar or baking soda to wash produce?

seo.title: Do you need vinegar or baking soda to wash produce?
seo.meta_description: Neither is required for routine produce washing. Running water and friction are the basics; vinegar and baking soda have variable effects and do not guarantee disinfection.
seo.search_intent: Determine whether vinegar or baking soda is needed for washing produce and distinguish pesticide removal from microbial safety.

excerpt: You do not need vinegar or baking soda for routine fruit and vegetable washing. Potable running water and friction are the basics. Some solutions can reduce particular residues under specific conditions, but they do not sterilize produce or work equally on every food.
content_html:
You do not need to turn the sink into a chemistry experiment to wash an apple or lettuce. For routine household produce washing, potable running water and friction are the basic recommendation. Vinegar and baking soda can affect certain residues or microbes under specific test conditions, but that does not make either one a required step or a guaranteed disinfectant.

“It worked in a study” does not mean “everyone needs to do it”

A washing solution works differently depending on concentration, contact time, temperature, produce surface, and the microbe or chemical residue being targeted. An unmeasured homemade splash does not automatically reproduce experimental conditions.

FDA guidance recommends washing produce thoroughly under running water and does not require vinegar, baking soda, or a commercial produce wash for routine household preparation.

Vinegar can reduce some bacteria, but it does not sterilize produce

Household-washing studies have measured microbial reductions with acidic solutions, but results vary greatly among lettuce, tomatoes, apples, cucumbers, and other surfaces. In one study, soaking lettuce in 5% vinegar before rinsing did not reduce an indicator bacterium significantly more than soaking in cold tap water.

Other experiments using different concentrations and contact times have found additional reductions. That variability is the point: “a splash of vinegar” is not a standardized sanitizing dose.

Baking soda has a different evidence base: some surface pesticides

An apple study using two experimentally applied pesticides found a baking-soda solution of 10 mg/mL, about 1%, removed surface residues more effectively than tap water under those test conditions. It took about 12–15 minutes to completely remove the tested surface residues.

The same experiment also showed the limitation: some pesticide had penetrated the apple peel and could not be washed away. The result does not show that baking soda removes every pesticide from every fruit or vegetable.

Pesticide removal and microbial safety are different questions

A solution can help with a chemical residue without being a reliable way to control pathogens. None of these washes substitutes for refrigeration, avoiding cross-contamination, discarding rotten produce, or cooking when appropriate.

Do not use dish soap or detergent

Soap is designed for hands or dishes, not to remain on porous food. The FDA specifically advises against using soap, detergent, or unvalidated commercial produce washes on fruits and vegetables.

So should you use vinegar or baking soda?

For ordinary produce at home: neither is required. Rinse under running water, rub the surface, brush firm produce, and dry with a clean towel or paper towel.

If public-health authorities issue a specific sanitizing instruction for an outbreak or particular product, follow that protocol rather than improvising concentrations. Routine washing does not need an acid-base experiment.

faq.question: Does vinegar disinfect fruits and vegetables?
faq.answer: It can reduce some microbes under specific conditions, but it does not sterilize produce and effectiveness depends on concentration, time, and food.

faq.question: Does baking soda remove pesticides?
faq.answer: It can help with some surface residues; one apple study used about a 1% solution for 12–15 minutes, but it did not remove pesticide that had penetrated the peel.

faq.question: What should you do routinely?
faq.answer: Rinse under potable running water, rub or brush firm surfaces, and dry with a clean towel or paper towel.
